Cardinals
kär´dĭ-nalz
n. pl. (the princes of the Roman church, ranking next below the pope and electing him)
Latin cardo, a hinge — the men on whom the government of the church is said to turn. The college took its present form in the eleventh century; the scarlet dates from the thirteenth.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The cardinals form a princely order within the church. Christ forbids the pattern by name: “ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them. But it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:25–26). He forbids the titles: “be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren… neither be ye called masters” (Mat 23:8–10). He inverts the ranking: “he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve” (Luk 22:26). Peter, whose successors they claim to advise, writes “neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3). And John names the type (3Jn 1:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines cardinal as an ecclesiastical prince in the Romish church, who has a voice in the conclave at the election of a pope; and cardinal as an adjective, chief, principal, preeminent, or fundamental.

expand to see more

CARDINAL, a. Chief, principal, preeminent, or fundamental; as the cardinal virtues, which pagans supposed to be justice, prudence, temperance and fortitude.

CARDINAL, n. An ecclesiastical prince in the Romish church, who has a voice in the conclave at the election of a pope, who is taken from their number.

The cardinals are divided into three classes, bishops, priests and deacons.

Key Scripture

Mat 20:25 — "But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them."

Mat 23:8 — "But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren."

Luk 22:26 — "But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve."

1Pe 5:3 — "Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock."

3Jn 1:9 — "I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not."

Modern Corruption

The court of a temporal prince is reproduced inside the church, and every tradition builds one eventually.

expand to see more

Luke 22:26 is the most damning setting for these verses, and it is worth remembering where the dispute occurred. The disciples were arguing about which of them should be accounted the greatest — at the Last Supper, after the bread and the cup, with the betrayal already in motion. The Lord's reply gives the whole doctrine of Christian office in two clauses: he that is greatest, as the younger; he that is chief, as he that doth serve. And then He says, I am among you as he that serveth, which is the only argument He offers.

Matthew 23:8–10 is not a wooden prohibition of every honorific — Paul calls himself a father to the Corinthians in the next breath after refusing to lord it over their faith — but a prohibition of a class of men set above the brotherhood by title. The clause that carries it is all ye are brethren. Whatever offices a church has, they operate inside a brotherhood, and the moment an office puts a man outside it, on a different footing before God, the arrangement has failed regardless of what it is called.

It is easy for a Protestant to read this entry as an attack on somebody else, and dishonest to leave it there. Every tradition grows a court. The celebrity pastor with an entourage and no one able to rebuke him, the conference platform that functions as a hierarchy without a constitution, the denominational office that outranks a congregation in practice while disclaiming it in theory — each is a college of cardinals without the scarlet. The test is not the vestment but the question Matthew 20 puts: is authority here exercised over people, or spent on them?

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek katakurieuo (G2634), to exercise lordship over; kathegetes (G2519), master, guide; adelphoi (G80), brethren; diakoneo (G1247), to serve.

Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to lord it over; Matthew 20:25, Mark 10:42, 1 Peter 5:3.

Greek kathegetes (G2519) — master, leader; Matthew 23:10 only.

Greek ho diakonon (G1247) — he that serveth; Luke 22:26–27.

Usage

"“But it shall not be so among you” — stated as a contrast of systems."

"“All ye are brethren” — the clause that carries the prohibition."

"“I am among you as he that serveth” — the only argument He offers."
